newsitem.title: BRAZIL: ACPC coffee members upbeat on response to Africans.
newsitem.headline: ACPC coffee members upbeat on response to Africans.

text.p: Members of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) are optimistic they will agree on a response to a call by African nations to cut member exports further in the first half of 1997, officials said after a Wednesday evening meeting.
"We had very positive discussions about the African proposal," said Herbert de Sola, El Salvador's representative to the ACPC.
"The underlying feeling is that there is goodwill from all parts to decide to do whatever is sensible," said Derek Watson, adviser to the Indonesian delegation.
Members were to discuss the issue again on Thursday at a meeting scheduled to begin at 1000 local/1200 GMT.

African nations have said they want a 2.5 million 60-kg bag reduction in ACPC member exports between January and June this year, which under a plan agreed in May last year should not exceed 26.28 million bags.
Earlier this week the Ugandan trade and industry minister said the 2.5 million bags would ideally involve a reduction of 1.5 million bags from arabica producers and one million bags from robustas.

But given the recent rise in arabica prices, now also being seen in robustas, many people at the three-day international coffee seminar that ended Wednesday in Rio de Janeiro said any need to address an imbalance between the two is rapidly disappearing.

Moreover, if one of the ACPC's long-stated goals is to create market stability and avoid sharp and often short-lived rallies, then the worst thing the ACPC could now do would be to announce a cut in exports at a time when the market is clearly showing tight supply, they said.
"That would look like market distortion which is the last thing the ACPC wants," one trader said.
"It would make no sense to cut exports at all at this point, no sense at all. If anything, they should be going the other way," said Jair Coser, president of Brazilian exporter Unicafe.

Producer representatives this evening did not want to speculate on whether they would eventually agree on a cut, saying they needed to analyse information on past exports and production that had only just been prepared.
Preliminary indications were ACPC members had complied with a limit of 27.27 million bags in the six months to December, de Sola said.
"It appears everything is in order," he told reporters.

But looking ahead, there is the possibility some groups may anyway be unable to meet their export targets even without cuts as is the case with African nations, Ugandan Trade and Industry Minister Abel Rwendeire said earlier this week.
Central American nations have also been revising down their production forecasts for a variety of reasons over the past weeks, posing a question mark over export potential.

Two other factors to be taken into consideration are growing consumption and less-than-expected non-ACPC member exports that had been forecast to reach around 20 million bags in 1996/97 (July/June) but now look to end nearer to 16.5 million bags, de Sola said.

Producers, therefore, may look to ensure that prices continue steadily on their current upward trend while both trying not to promote a sharp rally but also seeking to prevent a fall to levels that prompted the original call for export cuts in December.

This would be in line with comments made by the Ivory Coast's minister for commodities, Guy-Alain Gauze, who in a speech Wednesday to delegates welcomed the current firming in market prices at the seminar but stressed producer nations should not become heady in case the upward move is merely a prelude to a decline in prices.
One option, therefore, being considered is the use of indicative prices, a producer delegate said earlier today.

These would be different from trigger prices in that they could not be used by the market as an effective ceiling or floor but instead would be levels which if touched would involve the ACPC council reviewing the market situation to see if action was needed.
-- Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
